text: Graph-based predictive and prescriptive analytics for cross-border power grids
Data → Cleaning → Features → Forecasting → Evaluation → Graph reasoning → Scenario simulation → Recommendation
A complete, auditable workflow from raw hourly records to an explainable rerouting scenario

Opening: introduce the operational question. The project predicts the next-hour state of a cross-border network, explains which nodes and edges are under pressure, and tests a possible alternate route. Team members: Prakki Krishna Karthik, Vasudev, and Shubham Bhuyan. Faculty: Pattabiraman V.
Cross-border flow is a network problem, not a single-line problem. A local change can affect neighbouring countries and the routes available for recovery.
What is likely to happen in the next hour?
Forecast country net flow and load from recent time-series behaviour, global network context, and graph centrality.
What can we test when a link becomes stressed?
Remove a selected share of transfer, search connected alternate paths, check headroom and stress, and report the loss trade-off.
Data preprocessing  ·  time-series forecasting  ·  regression metrics  ·  classification metrics  ·  class imbalance  ·  model comparison  ·  decision support

Explain the distinction: predictive analytics estimates the future; prescriptive analytics evaluates an action. The project deliberately stops at recommendation because it lacks engineering-grade operating constraints.
The raw files contain more variables than the current experiment uses. The model keeps a deliberate 11-feature set so each prediction remains explainable.

Source: results/run_metadata.json and backend/experiments.py. Explain the difference in simple terms: Fusion GRU processes a country sequence with global context; DCRNN exchanges information through the graph at every recurrent step.
DCRNN keeps the node axis intact. At every hour, it diffuses information through the 12-country graph before applying a GRU-style update.

DCRNN worked example: how a neighbour affects a forecast
Imagine three connected countries. The same mechanism runs on all 12 countries in the actual experiment.
A_f B and A_r B carry one-hop information. Applying them again carries a two-hop signal. The recurrent gates then decide whether that neighbour signal should change the hidden state.

DCRNN is valuable because it tests the graph hypothesis. It lags here because topology is incomplete electrical information, neighbour signals can add noise, and the benchmark has limited engineering labels.

Source: results/model_comparison.json, results/dcrnn_analysis.json, and results/run_metadata.json. Use the three-node illustration only as a teaching example. The actual model processes 12 countries jointly and predicts the next net flow for every node.

MAE = (1/n) Σ |y − ŷ|

RMSE = √[(1/n) Σ (y − ŷ)²]

MAPE = (100/n) Σ |(y − ŷ) / y|
RMSE drives model selection. MAPE is included for completeness but becomes unstable when net flow is near zero or changes sign.

Precision = TP / (TP + FP)

Recall = TP / (TP + FN)

F1 = 2PR / (P + R)
The model converts continuous flow into Normal, Warning, and Critical classes using training-data thresholds. This exposes missed warnings, not only average MW error.

Classification evidence: confusion matrix and ROC/PR
Rows are actual classes. Columns are predicted classes. Off-diagonal cells expose missed warnings and false alarms.
ROC evaluates separability across thresholds. Precision–Recall is more informative when Critical cases are less frequent.

Graph intelligence: stress propagation and node influence

Two-step propagation combines local node risk with utilization-weighted neighbouring risk. Influence also includes graph centrality, so a bridge node can matter even before it becomes the most loaded node.

Source: results/figures/graph_stress_propagation.png and results/figures/graph_node_influence.png. The graph analysis is a transparent screening layer, not an AC power-flow or N-1 security calculation.
Edge resilience and stress over time
Criticality is more than current loading: it combines dynamic stress, edge betweenness, disconnected pairs after removal, and increased shortest-path length.

Source: results/figures/graph_resilience_ranking.png and results/figures/graph_stress_timeline.png. Explain that the ranking asks what the topology loses if an edge disappears, while the timeline shows how dynamic stress changes through replay.
Prescriptive routing: how the alternate path is chosen
Set a hypothetical reduction, capped at 60%.
Penalize distance, utilization, loss, and risk.
Show route, bottleneck, and loss delta.
Warning links receive a 1.35× penalty. Critical links receive a 4× penalty during soft scoring. Strict search first requires enough proxy headroom.
The result is a recommendation-only scenario. It never dispatches generation or switches a real line.

Findings, novelty, limitations, and next step
01  A messy cross-border dataset can become a canonical graph.
02  Chronological validation protects the forecast comparison.
03  A simple baseline remains a useful operational comparator.
04  Graph reasoning can explain node influence and edge resilience.
05  Rerouting can be tested with visible guardrails and loss trade-offs.
01  One auditable workflow joins predictive and prescriptive analysis.
02  Data quality, physical assumptions, and graph risk stay visible.
03  Stress propagation and counterfactual resilience add graph evidence.
04  The dashboard explains what the model can and cannot claim.
01  Replace proxy capacity with verified thermal ratings.
02  Add surveyed line geometry and actual electrical parameters.
03  Calibrate thresholds using engineering events or quantiles.
04  Connect the replay API to SCADA, Kafka, or MQTT telemetry.
05  Validate recommendations with AC power flow and N-1 studies.
Final takeaway: the model produces evidence for human review, not an automatic operating command.

Closing: return to the original question. The project connects data quality, predictive modelling, graph reasoning, and route simulation in one traceable workflow. The main contribution is the auditable integration and honest handling of missing engineering information.
